name: Calorie counting

image.caption: Interim Report on Calorie Counting Model

lead: Calorie counting means recording the energy in everything eaten to stay under or over a target. Looksmaxxers mostly use it to lose fat so the face and body look leaner, and in reverse for deliberate weight gain.

Holding intake below expenditure produces weight loss and above it weight gain, so counting gives precise control over cutting and bulking. Behavioural weight-management programmes have been meta-analysed; no study measures facial appearance outcomes directly.

paras: People log food with an app or food scale and estimate maintenance calories, then set a deficit or surplus and watch weekly weight. Energy values come from standard factors for protein, carbohydrate and fat, so numbers are estimates.

A 2017 study found associations between calorie tracking and eating-disorder symptoms, and tracking apps have been linked to such symptoms in some users. Label values are estimates and can differ from the energy a person absorbs.

chain: Leaner or fuller face and body
angle.text: Looksmaxxers count calories to control cutting and bulking precisely, mainly to get lean enough to show facial and body definition. Tracking is a studied aid to weight change; claims that it is the best route to a leaner face are user opinion.

lead: Calorie counting is the practice of logging the energy content of everything eaten, usually in kilocalories and often with a phone app or food scale, in order to hold intake above or below a target. In looksmaxxing communities it is mainly used for fat loss ("cutting") to reveal facial and body leanness, and in reverse for deliberate weight gain.

Food energy figures come from the Atwater system, which multiplies measured protein, carbohydrate and fat by standard energy factors rather than burning food directly. Reference works note that this yields estimates, not exact values, and that labelled energy can differ from what a given person absorbs.[1] Published research on tracking and weight management is mixed in focus: behavioural weight-management programmes have been meta-analysed, and some studies have examined links between calorie tracking and eating-disorder symptoms.[2][3]
infobox: Fat loss or weight gain via tracked energy intake
Food scales, nutrition labels, tracking apps

paras: Practitioners estimate daily energy needs, set a target relative to it, and weigh or measure foods to log them against that target. Food energy is conventionally expressed in kilocalories, where one kilocalorie equals 4.184 kilojoules, and values on labels are derived from the modified Atwater system using roughly 4 kcal per gram of protein and carbohydrate and 9 kcal per gram of fat.[1]
Nutrition labelling rules differ by country, and treatment of fibre and sugar alcohols varies between regulations, which can make labelled values differ.[1]

Within appearance-focused communities, counting is discussed as a tool for lowering body-fat percentage so that jawline, cheekbones and under-eye area are more visible, and as the companion of bulking phases when gaining weight. It is commonly paired with protein targets and resistance training.

A systematic review and meta-regression of behavioural weight-management programmes examined which programme techniques and delivery modes were associated with greater mean weight loss in overweight and obese adults.[2] A separate meta-analysis on eating attentively examined how memory and awareness of food intake affect how much is eaten.[3]
A randomised trial of time-restricted eating without calorie counting reported weight outcomes in a racially diverse population, illustrating approaches that avoid explicit tracking.[4]

A 2017 study in Eating Behaviors examined associations between calorie counting, fitness-tracking technology and eating-disorder symptoms.[5] Clinicians and researchers have raised this association as a consideration for people prone to disordered eating.

No trials were found that test calorie counting specifically for facial appearance outcomes. Related human research includes behavioural weight-management meta-analyses and randomised trials of time-restricted eating, which address body weight rather than facial aesthetics.[2][4]

lore.intro: Calorie counting is a baseline practice in cutting and bulking discussions in fitness and looksmaxxing spaces.

claims.claim: Tracking calories precisely is the most reliable route to a leaner face.
Counting is unnecessary because meal timing alone can produce loss.
Constant tracking can become unhealthy for some people.
